title: Memory: fast, small, forgetful
story:
A processor can perform an operation in well under a nanosecond. Fetching the operand from main memory takes on the order of a hundred. That ratio is the single most important number in this track, because almost every performance surprise in a well-written program traces back to it.

It is also getting worse, and worse in a specific way. Wulf and McKee named the problem in 1995: processor speed and memory speed both improve exponentially, but the exponent for microprocessors is substantially larger than that for DRAMs, and because the difference between diverging exponentials also grows exponentially, an already-existing disparity becomes a much bigger problem over time. Their point was not that memory is slow — it was that the gap widens by construction, so any design that waits for memory ages badly on purpose. That paper is where the term memory wall comes from.

The shape of the response is a hierarchy. A small, fast store sits next to the processor holding what was used recently, a larger and slower one sits behind it, then main memory, then the persistent store. Each level is a bet that what you touched recently you will touch again, and that what sits beside it you will touch soon. Those two bets are temporal and spatial locality, and the hierarchy is worth its enormous complexity only to the extent that programs honour them.

Which is the point worth carrying out of this lesson, because it is the one that changes how you write code. The hierarchy is not a speed-up applied uniformly. It is a speed-up conditional on access pattern. A program that walks memory in order gets nearly the speed of the fast level, because each slow fetch brings in a block that serves the next several accesses. A program that jumps unpredictably gets nearly the speed of the slow level while paying for all the machinery of the fast one — and the two programs can be identical in every respect that a complexity analysis would notice.

The general pattern is the one Patterson documented later across four technologies: bandwidth improves much more quickly than latency, with bandwidth improving by more than the square of the improvement in latency. The hierarchy exists precisely to convert a latency problem into a bandwidth problem, by fetching more than you asked for in the hope you will want it.

problem.name: The memory hierarchy
problem.shape: The processor consumes data far faster than the store holding it can supply, and the gap widens every year.
tell: a loop is far slower than its operation count suggests
the data structure is built from pointers scattered across memory
two algorithms with the same complexity differ by an order of magnitude
performance falls off a cliff as the working set grows
problem.move: Arrange work so that memory is touched in a predictable order and repeatedly within a short window. Prefer contiguous layouts to pointer-chasing, size the working set to fit a level of the hierarchy where possible, and measure rather than reason about which level you are hitting.
problem.invariant: Each level bets that recently used data will be used again and that neighbouring data will be used soon. The hierarchy pays off exactly to the degree those two bets hold.
problem.breaks: The bet fails silently. An access pattern with no locality is served correctly and at the speed of the slow level, with the fast level's cost still paid — so the failure appears as a performance mystery rather than as an error, and nothing in the code distinguishes the good case from the bad.

cost.time: nothing when locality holds; up to two orders of magnitude when it does not
cost.space: fetching a whole block to serve one byte, which is wasted bandwidth when the rest goes unused
cost.beats: a flat uniform memory, which would have to run at the speed of the slowest part

worked.problem: Why can the same loop, over the same amount of data, run an order of magnitude slower depending on the order of access?
worked.reasoning:
Because the cost of a memory access is not a property of the access, it is a property of where the data already happens to be — and the order you touch things in decides that.

Start from the ratio. An operation takes well under a nanosecond; a fetch from main memory takes on the order of a hundred. A hierarchy exists to hide that, and it hides it by two bets: that data used recently will be used again, and that data beside it will be used soon.

The second bet is the one order of access decides. Memory is not fetched a byte at a time — a miss brings in a whole block. Walk an array in order and one slow fetch serves the next several accesses, so the cost is amortised and you run near the speed of the fast level. Jump around unpredictably and every access misses, every miss fetches a block of which you use one item, and you run near the speed of the slow level while the machinery of the fast one is still being paid for.

That is the whole mechanism, and it explains why two implementations that a complexity analysis cannot distinguish differ by a factor of ten. The analysis counts operations and treats every memory access as one unit of cost. The hardware charges between one and a hundred depending on history.

The structural reason this matters more each year rather than less is the divergence: processor and memory speeds both improve exponentially with different exponents, so the difference between diverging exponentials grows exponentially too. A design that waits on memory does not merely perform badly, it performs worse over time.

What I would actually do about it is concrete. Prefer contiguous layouts over structures built from pointers, because pointer-chasing is the canonical no-locality pattern. Iterate in the order the data is laid out rather than the order that reads naturally — which for a two-dimensional array means matching the storage order rather than fighting it. And where the working set can be made to fit inside a level, block the computation so that it does.

The broader framing is that a hierarchy converts a latency problem into a bandwidth problem, fetching more than you asked for in the hope you will want it. That trade is favourable because bandwidth improves much faster than latency — by more than the square, as a rule of thumb — so it is worth wasting bandwidth to avoid waiting. Access order determines whether you get that trade or merely pay for it.

problem.practice: Sum a large two-dimensional array twice, once walking it in the order it is stored and once across that order, and time both. The operation count is identical. Then grow the array until the slower version's time jumps, and note where that happened.

beats.broke: The processor can consume data far faster than the store holding it can supply, and the gap has widened every year rather than closing.
beats.fix: Arrange storage as a hierarchy — a small fast level beside the processor holding what was used recently or lies next to it, with progressively larger and slower levels behind.
beats.cost: The hierarchy pays only when access has locality, so a program touching memory unpredictably gets the speed of the slow level while paying for all the machinery of the fast one.

interview.q: Why can the same loop, over the same amount of data, run an order of magnitude slower depending on the order of access?
interview.trap: Looking for a difference in the algorithm. The operation counts can be identical — what differs is whether each slow fetch serves one access or several, and a complexity analysis cannot see that distinction at all.
interview.answer:
Because the cost of a memory access is a property of where the data already is, not of the access — and access order decides that.

The ratio to start from: an operation takes well under a nanosecond and a main-memory fetch takes on the order of a hundred. The hierarchy hides that with two bets — that recently used data will be used again, and that neighbouring data will be used soon.

Order decides the second bet. Memory is not fetched a byte at a time; a miss brings in a whole block. Walk an array in order and one slow fetch serves the next several accesses, so you run near the speed of the fast level. Jump unpredictably and every access misses, each miss fetches a block of which you use one item, and you run near the slow level while still paying for the fast one's machinery.

That is why two implementations a complexity analysis cannot separate differ by a factor of ten: the analysis treats every memory access as one unit of cost, and the hardware charges between one and a hundred depending on history.

It also gets worse rather than better. Processor and memory speeds both improve exponentially with different exponents, so the difference between diverging exponentials grows exponentially — a design that waits on memory ages badly by construction.

Practically: prefer contiguous layouts over pointer-chasing, iterate in the order the data is laid out rather than the order that reads naturally, and block the computation so the working set fits inside a level where it can.

The framing I would offer is that a hierarchy converts a latency problem into a bandwidth problem — fetching more than you asked for in the hope you will want it — which is a good trade because bandwidth improves far faster than latency. Access order decides whether you receive that trade or only pay for it.
